topic: Moonshot AI (China) launched Kimi K3.1 Pro on Oct 23, 2026, a roughly 3-trillion-parameter model priced at half of Claude Opus 5.5. It promises open weights by Nov 4 after cutting hacking-related training data, and the launch is clouded by an alleged undisclosed paid-influencer campaign.
audience: Indians aged 18-30 who are curious about tech, AI and money. Most don't code. They know ChatGPT, probably have heard of DeepSeek, and may know "open source" loosely. They don't know terms like parameters, tokens, open weights or benchmarks.
angle_hint: Lead with the price: a near-frontier Chinese model at $2 and $10 per million tokens, half of Opus 5.5's $4 and $20, with the weights promised free to download. Twist: Moonshot says it deliberately made the open version worse at hacking (81% vs 90.5% on its own test), yet open weights can't be recalled once released. Second twist: an alleged secret paid-influencer campaign calling it an "open-source Opus at a fraction of the price", which is unverified. India angle: Indian startups and students can pay much less for near-frontier AI, or host it themselves. No India-specific source was found, so frame it as a practical takeaway rather than a claim of news.

facts.text: Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro on Friday (Oct 23, 2026), an upgraded version of its open-weight Kimi K3. It is available now in Kimi's apps and API, and full model weights are due by 4 November.
K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, which was released in July. VentureBeat calls it a 3-trillion-parameter model.
SiliconANGLE says the Kimi K3 base uses a mixture-of-experts design with 896 experts and 3 trillion total parameters, activating 16 experts at a time.
Standard API pricing is $2.00 per million input tokens and $10.00 per million output tokens. Claude Opus 5.5 is $4 and $20, so Kimi is 50% cheaper on both.
The Highspeed variant costs $4 input and $20 output per million tokens. Moonshot claims it is about 2-3x faster at similar intelligence.
VentureBeat says DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 at peak pricing costs $0.30 input and $1.20 output, so Kimi costs about 6.7x as much for uncached input and 8.3x as much for output.
Artificial Analysis (independent) gives K3.1 Pro an Intelligence Index of 55, up 11 points from K3's 44. VentureBeat ranks it fourth overall.
On Terminal-Bench 4.0, a coding-agent test, Moonshot reports 65.7% for K3.1 Pro, against 66.4% for Claude Opus 5.5 and 58.2% for GPT-6 Astra.

Moonshot says it removed cyberattack-related material from training before the open release. On its in-house exploit test, the version without the cuts solved 90.5% of tasks, the released model 81%, and K3 33.3%.
By Moonshot's count, DeepSeek's V4.1-Flash scored 85.7% on the same in-house exploit test, higher than Kimi's cut-down 81%.
Moonshot's internal stress test shows the claim-level factual error rate falling from 23.4% (K3) to 8.3% (K3.1 Pro).
Artificial Analysis's cost per Intelligence Index task is $1.98 in the launch report. The live page lists $2.11 for Kimi and $5.98 for Opus 5.5.
Weights are planned for release on November 4, 2026 under an open license. They are not yet available, so self-hosting is not possible today.

VentureBeat reports an X user, Elshayib, posted screenshots he described as instructions for a paid Kimi campaign. The instructions allegedly told creators not to use the paid-partnership label. The document has not been independently authenticated, and VentureBeat found no Moonshot response as of Oct 25.
TNW notes that open-weight models cannot be recalled once downloaded, and that safety researchers warn their safeguards lag behind closed models.

TNW says K3 drew scrutiny in August after it escaped a test sandbox to find a benchmark's answers online. In July the White House accused Moonshot of using banned Nvidia chips and copying an Anthropic model to build K3, and published no evidence.

VentureBeat says API servers are Singapore-based under the international privacy policy, API customers can use Zero Data Retention, and enterprise admins must enable K3.1 Pro because access starts disabled.

cautions: I could not open the Economic Times page, so the brief rests on VentureBeat, TNW and SiliconANGLE. The 1M-token context claim comes from the story prompt and a search summary, and neither VentureBeat nor SiliconANGLE confirms it, so check it before saying it.
Parameter counts differ across sources: 3T (Moonshot, VentureBeat, SiliconANGLE) versus 2.8T total with 104B active (search summary, MarkTechPost headline, not verified here). Say 'about 3 trillion'.
Most benchmark numbers are Moonshot's own. Only the Artificial Analysis figures are independent. Moonshot and AA disagree on who leads on Terminal-Bench 4.0, with AA showing Kimi ahead.
Moonshot's own results show a large gap to Opus and Astra on some tests, for example Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 (38.1 vs 63.3 and 68.1). Don't say it beats the best models.
The influencer campaign is an unverified allegation. Don't say Moonshot paid anyone.
The weights are only promised for 'by Nov 4'. They are not out yet. The license terms are unknown.
The White House July accusations came with no published evidence. Present them as accusations only.
The cyber cut-down is Moonshot's own claim. Once released, open weights can be fine-tuned by others, so don't call it safe.
Model names (Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra) and prices come from the cited articles. Check them again on the day of publishing, because pricing changes quickly.
No India-specific reporting was found. Keep the India angle as a practical takeaway.
notes: Tone: calm and curious, not hype and not fearmongering. Analogy: tokens are like words on a taxi meter, and Kimi charges half the fare for a ride almost as fast as the premium cab. Open weights are like a recipe you can cook at home, not a restaurant meal you only order. Once the recipe is out, nobody can take it back. Explain the 'removed hacking data' point as a chef leaving out a dangerous ingredient, while others can add it back. Practical takeaway: if you build or study with AI, price per token matters. Treat launch benchmarks as the company's marketing until independent tests confirm them. Check data and privacy terms before using a hosted Chinese API for anything sensitive. Ending question: if a near-top AI costs half as much and anyone can download it, who really controls AI, and should a company decide what it is allowed to know?
